scenarios.question: What if the other person disputes your account?
scenarios.effect: Identify exactly which event or statement is disputed.
scenarios.preparation: Separate what you observed from what you infer. Identify any original record and say clearly when you are unsure.

procedure.label: Deciding what to do
procedure.guidance: Write down what happened, where and when, and the outcome you want. Use the possible provisions below to decide what to clarify next.

evidence_plan.heading: Evidence plan
prompts: Which part of the timeline needs independent support?
What already shows that event, and who may lawfully hold another record?

suggestions.title: Possession, title and notices
suggestions.look_for: Gather records you already hold, such as agreements, deeds, orders, rent payments or notices. Note who occupied the property and when that changed.
suggestions.why: Documents and the timeline can help distinguish possession from a claim about legal ownership.
suggestions.action: Keep full copies and record where each came from. Request records through the issuing office or a lawyer when needed.

suggestions.title: Location and visible changes
suggestions.look_for: Note the address or boundary reference and any changed lock, barrier or damage you actually observed.
suggestions.why: This helps identify the location and the particular change in dispute.
suggestions.action: Document only from an area you may safely and lawfully access. Do not enter disputed space or confront anyone.

suggestions.title: Original records and an evidence log
suggestions.look_for: Keep records you lawfully have, with their surrounding context. For each item note the related event, who provided it, when you received it, and any transfer.
suggestions.why: The log distinguishes what you observed from what someone later told you and makes it easier to check the source.
suggestions.action: Keep an unchanged original and label working copies. Avoid editing originals, guessing gaps, or sharing evidence publicly.

6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property .—(1) If any person is dispossessed without 
his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person 3[through whom 
                                                           
1. The words "except the State of Jammu and Kashmir" omitted by Act 34 of 2019, s. 95  and 96 and the Fifth Schedule                            
(w.e.f. 31-10-2019). 
2. 1st March, 196 4, vide notification No. S.O. 189, dated 1 3th January, 196 4, see Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II,                             
sec. 3(ii). 
3. Ins. by Act 18 of 2018, s. 2 (w.e.f. 1-10-2018). 
5 
 
he has been in possession or  any person] claiming through him may, by suit , recover possession thereof, 
notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. 
(2) No suit under this section shall be brought— 
(a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or 
(b) against the Government. 
(3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor 
shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed. 
(4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to 
recover possession thereof.

sources.title: Specific Relief Act, 1963
sources.text:
34. Discretion of court as to declaration of status or right .—Any person entitled to any legal 
character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested 
to deny, his title to such character or right, and the  court may in its discretion make therein a declaration 
that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief: 
Provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further 
relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so. 
14 
 
Explanation.—A trustee of property is a “person interested to deny” a title adverse to the title of some 
one who is not inexistence, and for whom, if in existence, he would be a trustee.

sources.title: Specific Relief Act, 1963
sources.text:
38. Perpetual injunction when granted.—(1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred 
to by this Chapter, a  perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an 
obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. 
(2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions 
contained in Chapter II. 
(3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, 
the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— 
(a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; 
(b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, 
by the invasion; 
(c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; 
(d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.
